input: Build a personal knowledge management system in Obsidian

keyUnknowns.whyItMatters: Obsidian can serve wildly different purposes — note-taking, project management, journaling, research, a second brain — and the scope determines which vaults, folders, and note types to build.
Whether this is purely personal or shared with a team changes sync strategy, permissions, and how notes are structured and named.
The user's domain (e.g., software engineering, academic research, creative writing) heavily shapes which templates, tags, and linking conventions make sense.
Time available to set up and maintain the system affects how elaborate the structure should be — a complex system that won't be maintained is worse than a simple one that will.
Some people prefer rigid folder hierarchies, others prefer tag-based or link-based (MOC/Zettelkasten) systems; this fundamentally changes the architecture.
Knowing which plugins (if any) are already installed or desired — e.g., Dataview, Templater, Kanban — determines what features can be built and which steps come first.
Without knowing what 'done well' looks like — fast retrieval, daily journaling habit, connected ideas, project tracking — it's impossible to prioritise which parts of the system matter most.

gold.taskTitle: Build a personal knowledge management system in Obsidian
gold.taskDescription: Set up a structured, functional PKM system inside Obsidian tailored to the user's specific knowledge work and goals.

questions.title: What subject area or type of work is this vault for?
questions.description: Identify the primary domain — e.g., software development, academic research, creative writing, business — so templates, tags, and note structures fit real content.

questions.title: What is the main purpose you want this system to serve?
questions.description: Clarify the core use case — e.g., capturing fleeting ideas, managing projects, writing long-form content, building a second brain — to define the vault's architecture.

questions.title: Will this vault be just for you or shared with others?
questions.description: Determine if the system is purely personal or needs to support collaboration, which affects sync tools, folder conventions, and naming standards.

questions.title: Do you prefer folders, tags, or links to organise notes?
questions.description: Establish the preferred organisational philosophy — rigid folder hierarchy, tag-based taxonomy, or link/MOC-based (Zettelkasten) — as this is the single biggest architectural decision.

questions.title: Which Obsidian plugins are you open to using?
questions.description: Find out if the user wants a core-only setup or is willing to use community plugins like Dataview, Templater, or Kanban, which unlock significantly different capabilities.

questions.title: How much time can you invest in setup and daily maintenance?
questions.description: Gauge available time to calibrate system complexity — a user with 30 minutes a week needs a very different system than someone willing to invest hours in curation.

questions.title: How will you know this system is actually working well for you?
questions.description: Define the success criteria — e.g., finding any note in under 10 seconds, writing a daily journal consistently, connecting ideas across projects — to set clear priorities.
